name: Vera Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, political parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at the Coolabah bauxite mine. That's the long machine with the blade underneath, and my job is keeping the haul roads smooth so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres or tip. I start at a quarter to six, say a prayer in the car park, do my checks and then it's up and down the roads all day, cutting the ruts and filling the potholes. I've been at it three years. Before that I raised four children and kept the books for our church.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to the mine at fifty-five?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Hiro worked at Coolabah for thirty years, on the shovels. He hurt his back badly and couldn't go back, so I asked the superintendent if there was anything for me, and he gave me a go on the grader. I like that the roads are a thing you can see, smooth or not, no arguing about it. What's hard is the new screens they keep putting in the cab, and feeling the young ones watching me take twice as long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that'd be a mercy. I've had enough change in the last few years to last me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad common sense won out. A machine is only as good as the person running it, that's what Hiro always said. I'd say it at church morning tea and at smoko, that's our break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I get to finish the job properly. I want to work until Hiro's settlement and our savings are enough that we never have to ask anyone for anything. Maybe another five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Same shift, same roads, same savings. We tithe to the church and put the rest of what's left over into the account. I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really. Like a dry harvest after a wet year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've had enough change. What change has been hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hiro's injury, first. Then going to work at fifty-five in a place full of men half my age. Then every few months they add something to the grader, a new screen, a camera, a tablet for the pre-start checks. I've got a little notebook with the steps written in, because I can't keep them in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would agree with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of the older operators. Col on the water truck, he's been there since the mine opened, he'd shake my hand. The young engineers wouldn't. They're nice boys but they think everything can be done better with a computer.

S0.say: She's glad common sense won, because a machine is only as good as the person running it. She'd say it at church morning tea and on the work break.
S0.think: I get to finish the job properly and work about five more years until Hiro's settlement and our savings mean we never have to ask anyone for anything.
S0.do: Keeps the same shifts, roads and savings. Keeps tithing to the church and putting the rest into savings.
S0.feel: Calm and thankful, like a dry harvest after a wet year.
S0.quote: I've got a little notebook with the steps written in, because I can't keep them in my head.
S0.fieldNote: Vera came to mining out of necessity after her husband's injury and sees the job as a duty. Her faith and self-reliance are central; she wants never to depend on anyone. She finds each new screen in the cab a real burden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's already started. They've put the GPS thing on two of the graders, where the blade sets its own height.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a company has every right to run its mine the way it wants. But I'd also say they should look after the people who've been loyal. That's just decency, and I'd say it to the superintendent if he asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm the one they'd let go. I'm slow, I'm new, and I can't work the screens the way the young ones can. With Hiro off work, I'm the one bringing the money in, and I know that's a weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my son-in-law, Ben, he's good with computers, to sit with me on Sunday afternoons and go through the new screens until I've got them. I'd make sure I'm never late, never sick, never complaining. And I'd start putting a bit less in the account for extras and cut back on the little things, so we're ready if it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. I'd still sleep, but I'd be saying an extra prayer at night. I don't like feeling like the weak link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't keep the steps in your head. Would Sunday afternoons with Ben really help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. He's patient, more patient than the trainers at work, who talk too fast. I'd rather learn from family than from a stranger with a clipboard. And if it doesn't stick, well, I tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaway on Friday nights, probably, and the new caravan Hiro has been looking at. We'd hold off on that. We don't need it, it's just a want. Hiro would grumble, but he'd understand.

S1.say: A company has every right to run its mine as it wants, but it should look after loyal people. That's simple decency.
S1.think: I'm slow, new and weak on the screens, so I'd be the one let go. With Hiro off work I bring the money in, and that's a weak spot.
S1.do: Asks her son-in-law to go through the new screens with her on Sunday afternoons and makes sure she's never late, sick or complaining. Cuts back on extras like Friday takeaway and puts off a caravan.
S1.feel: Worried but still sleeping, with an extra prayer at night and a dislike of being the weak link.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn from family than from a stranger with a clipboard.
S1.fieldNote: Even moderate change puts real pressure on Vera because she's the household earner and struggles with new technology. She respects the company's rights while appealing to loyalty and decency. Her instinct is to lean on family, not training schemes or government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Lord. No. That's too fast for anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should stick together, families and churches, because the government won't save us and I wouldn't want it to. I'd say we've been through droughts and floods in this town and we'll get through this. That's what I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. The grader is the easiest thing to put a robot on, it's just roads, it's just the same roads every day. I'd lose my job within a year, and Hiro can't work. We've got savings, but I was counting on five more years to make it enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every extra spending straight away and keep working until they hand me the letter. I'd talk to our daughter about whether we could move in with them later on, or they with us, to share costs. I'd ask the pastor if the church could start some kind of help for families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. I'd be up in the night. I'd be praying a lot. It feels like the ground going out from under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with more warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't get my five years. With five or ten, I could at least finish what I started and build the savings up. With two, I'm out before we're ready, and I'm too old to start something else. There's no time to even get used to the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't want the government to save you. If there were government help, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a hard one. I don't believe in handouts, I never have. But if Hiro needed something and it was there, I suppose I'd swallow my pride. I'd hate it, though. I'd rather it came from the church or the family.

S2.say: Families and churches should stick together, because the government won't save them and she wouldn't want it to. The town has survived droughts and floods before.
S2.think: The grader is the easiest machine to automate, so she'd lose her job within a year with Hiro unable to work. The savings fall short of what five more years would have built.
S2.do: Stops all extra spending at once and works until she gets the letter. Talks with her daughter about sharing a home to cut costs and asks the pastor to set up church help for families who lose work.
S2.feel: Frightened and praying through the night, as if the ground were going out from under her.
S2.quote: The grader is the easiest thing to put a robot on, it's just roads, it's just the same roads every day.
S2.fieldNote: Her strong savings don't calm her because she's the only earner and planned on five more years to make them enough. Her public line is communal resilience; privately she's frightened. Asked gently about government help, she admitted she'd take it for her husband, though she'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but that's more like it. I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families need to plan and save, and companies should give their loyal workers a fair warning and a fair payout. People should look after themselves first and then their neighbours. That's how it's always been done here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is close to what I need. I'd lose a little, maybe a year, but Hiro's settlement and what we've saved would just about see us through. It's still a worry, but it's not the end of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving harder than ever, maybe skip the tithe increase this year and put it in the account. I'd keep going with Ben on Sundays so I can at least keep up until the robots come. And I'd tell the kids not to expect help from us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried still, but I can breathe. It's like knowing the flood's coming but having time to move the furniture upstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the two-year picture you'd be up at night. What's different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to finish. Three more years is three more years of pay and savings. That's the difference between asking our children for help and not asking. I'd rather never ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip the tithe increase. That seems like a big thing for you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. I've never cut back on the church. But the Lord gave us sense too, and I think He'd understand. I'd make it up later if we could.

S3.say: Families need to plan and save, and companies should give loyal workers fair warning and a fair payout. People look after themselves first, then their neighbours.
S3.think: Five years is close to what she needs; she'd lose maybe a year, but the settlement and savings would just about see them through.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves harder, putting this year's planned tithe increase into savings instead. Keeps learning the screens with her son-in-law on Sundays and tells her children not to expect help for a while.
S3.feel: Still worried but able to breathe, like having time to move furniture upstairs before a flood.
S3.quote: That's the difference between asking our children for help and not asking. I'd rather never ask.
S3.fieldNote: For Vera, warning time is measured in whether she has to ask her children for help. Skipping the tithe increase is a telling sacrifice that shows how seriously she takes the threat. She stays anxious but feels in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'll be done by then, God willing. Sitting on the veranda with Hiro.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any family to get ready if they're sensible. Young people should learn a real trade and work hard. I'd say that to my grandchildren and to the young ones at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's alright. I'd finish my five years and stop at sixty-three, with our savings in good shape. What worries me is the grandchildren, and the church, if half the town has no work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving as planned and retire at sixty-three. I'd help the church run a small fund for families who struggle. And I'd tell the grandchildren to learn something with their hands that people will still pay for, like their grandfather did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A worry for the grandkids, but that's what grandmothers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there anything you'd do now that you wouldn't with less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop worrying about the screens so much. With ten years, I'd be retired before the robots, so I just need to be good enough to finish. With two years, I'd be scrambling. With ten I can let it go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on trades, but the card says robots reach hands-on work too. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I suppose I just don't believe a robot can do everything a person does, not properly. Maybe that's me being old-fashioned. I'd still tell them to work hard and be honest, because that's never wrong.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for any sensible family to get ready, and young people should learn a real trade and work hard.
S4.think: She'd finish her five years and stop at sixty-three with savings in good shape. Her worry is for her grandchildren and the church if half the town has no work.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving and retires at sixty-three as planned. Helps the church run a small fund for struggling families and urges her grandchildren to learn hands-on skills.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with the ordinary worry of a grandmother.
S4.quote: With two years, I'd be scrambling. With ten I can let it go.
S4.fieldNote: A decade's warning lets her stop fighting the screens because she'd retire before the robots arrive. Challenged on hands-on trades, she admitted she doesn't know and falls back on her belief in hard work and honesty. Her concern turns to the church and the next generation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. I'd be out before we were ready, with Hiro not able to work. What would help is the company giving loyal workers a proper payout and a bit of notice, and the church and families having the means to look after each other. I don't want a cheque from the government, I want a fair go from the people I work for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People think it's old-fashioned, but it's what gets you through when the ground moves. Whatever happens with these robots, I'll still be in church on Sunday.

headlineQuote: I don't want a cheque from the government, I want a fair go from the people I work for.
portrait: Vera Tanaka is a 58-year-old grader operator at a bauxite mine who started three years ago, after raising four children, when her husband's back injury ended his thirty years on the shovels. She is now the household earner, devout, self-reliant and firmly against handouts, and she struggles with every new screen in her cab. She is calm if AI stalls but anxious even with steady change, because she sees herself as the weak link. AGI in two years alarms her because the grader is easy to automate and she'd lose the five years she planned on, while five or ten years of warning let her finish and lean on family and church rather than the state.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because she'd be out of work before they were ready, with her husband unable to work.
whatWouldHelp: A proper payout and notice from the company for loyal workers, and churches and families having the means to look after each other, rather than a government cheque.
